questions: Does the RC actually still contain the client-IP-spoofing/collapse bug EV-034 describes, or was it already fixed and covered by a test?
What does application.yml actually set server.forward-headers-strategy to, and is there a boot-time guard against the vulnerable value?
Does AuthRateLimitFilter's clientIp() trust a client-supplied header directly, or only getRemoteAddr()?
Does a regression test exist for spoofed X-Forwarded-For, and does it pass when executed against the RC?
Does RazorpayX's payout API ever actually emit a status literally named 'failed', or is that premise wrong for this integration?
Which payout webhook event types does RazorpayWebhookController actually route, and do any map to an unhandled 'failed' status?
Does PayoutReconciliationService.attemptGatewayPayout really treat ANY exception as a definitive failure, and does it re-credit the wallet on that path?

Is there a compensating control (idempotency-key reuse, a get-payout-status reconciliation, terminal-state guard) that prevents a later genuine success webhook from causing a double payment after that reversal?
Does Payout.confirmStatus() prevent an already-terminal status (e.g. reversed) from being overwritten by a later conflicting webhook?
Does AdminCreatorAgentController#setMonthlyCap carry any role-tier (SUPER_ADMIN/ADMIN/SUPPORT) or MFA check, at the controller or service layer?
Is admin JWT authority ('ROLE_ADMIN') a single blanket role, or does it already encode the AdminRole tier (SUPER_ADMIN/ADMIN/SUPPORT) so hasRole('ADMIN') alone would exclude lower tiers?
Does this codebase have an established convention (AdminContextService.requireRoleWithMfaSatisfied) for gating sensitive admin mutations, and does this endpoint follow it?
Does the existing unit test for this controller assert or contradict the missing-gate claim?

findings.title: deploy/utho proxy chain likely collapses every client IP to the Docker gateway, making per-IP limits global
findings.reason: The exact defect class EV-034 hypothesizes was already found, fixed and load-bearing-documented in the RC. nginx sets X-Forwarded-For via $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for (appends, never overwrites) and Caddy's reverse_proxy likewise appends the true peer rather than replacing the header, so the chain is intact end-to-end. application.yml:90 pins `server.forward-headers-strategy: native` (NOT `framework`), which installs Tomcat's RemoteIpValve; the 40-line comment at application.yml:75-89 explicitly walks through why `framework`'s ForwardedHeaderFilter (trusts the LEFT-MOST, client-spoofable XFF entry, no trusted-proxy validation, strips headers) was the vulnerable configuration, and why `native`'s RemoteIpValve (validates against `internal-proxies`, walks XFF RIGHT-TO-LEFT skipping recognized internal proxies) is correct. application.yml:117's `internal-proxies` regex covers every RFC1918 range (10.x, 192.168.x, 169.254.x, 127.x, 172.16-31.x) that the Docker bridge network here would use, so Caddy's/nginx's own hop IPs are correctly skipped when resolving the true client. AuthRateLimitFilter.clientIp() (line ~704) simply returns `request.getRemoteAddr()` — no header is read by application code at all, so nothing downstream can be fed a forged value. SecretsStartupValidator (~line 547-551) refuses to boot outside dev if `forward-headers-strategy` is not `native`, closing the misconfiguration path EV-034's config-only review could not rule out. Most importantly, `AuthRateLimitFilterSpoofedForwardedForTest` is a targeted regression test for precisely this attack (rotating XFF from one real peer, and a genuinely different peer keeping its own bucket) and it is not aspirational — I ran it.
findings.new_evidence: Executed `cd influora-api && mvn -q -o -Dtest=AuthRateLimitFilterSpoofedForwardedForTest test` inside the clean RC checkout. Exit code 0. surefire report: `Tests run: 3, Failures: 0, Errors: 0`. This directly demonstrates: (1) a rotating spoofed X-Forwarded-For from one attacker peer cannot buy extra login attempts (429 after the limit, even with a fresh forged header or none at all), and (2) a genuinely different peer is NOT lumped into the same bucket even when it sends a colliding forged XFF — i.e. the exact 'one attacker collapses everyone into global 429s' scenario EV-034 worried about is the second test case, and it passes. Combined with the config/boot-guard evidence, this is CONFIRMED-RUNTIME refuted, not merely inferred.
findings.caveats: This refutes the mechanism EV-034 describes (IP-based rate limiting can be evaded by/collapsed via header spoofing). It does not evaluate whether Cloudflare or another edge in front of these domains could cause many distinct real users to legitimately share one apparent client IP (a different, minor, non-security correctness concern, not the P1 'one attacker triggers platform-wide 429s' claim made here).

findings.title: RazorpayX 'failed' status not treated as failure; any gateway exception treated as definitive failure and re-credited
findings.reason: The finding conflates two separate claims and only one survives. (1) 'failed status not treated as failure' — REFUTED as stated: RazorpayX payouts do not have a 'failed' status in this integration at all. RazorpayWebhookController's switch (lines 109-110) routes only `payout.processed`/`payout.reversed`/`payout.rejected`/`payout.cancelled`; `statusFromEventType` (255-263) maps exactly those four event types and nothing else; `PayoutReconciliationService.FAILURE_STATUSES` (63-64) is `{reversed, rejected, cancelled}` — an exhaustive, deliberately-broadened set per its own comment (the admin payout-retry bug it fixed). No code path ever receives or checks a literal 'failed' string, so there is no such status silently falling through. (2) 'any gateway exception treated as definitive failure and re-credited' — CONFIRMED as written: `attemptGatewayPayout` (237-268) wraps `razorpayXClient.initiatePayout(...)` in a bare `catch (Exception e)` and unconditionally marks the payout REVERSED and re-credits the creator's wallet on ANY exception (network timeout, malformed response, etc.), with no check of RazorpayX's actual current status via a GET/fetch call. `Payout.confirmStatus()` (306-315) has zero guard against overwriting an already-terminal status, so if a later genuine `payout.processed` webhook for the same id ever arrived after this reversal, nothing would stop it flipping the row to 'processed' while the earlier wallet re-credit stands uncorrected — a theoretical double-payment. However, severity is lower than claimed for two reasons: (a) the ONLY caller of this exception-guarded path today is the 15-minute orphaned-debit sweep and the admin retry path, and the sweep deliberately reuses the SAME idempotency key as the original attempt specifically so a call that actually already succeeded at RazorpayX returns the same successful result instead of throwing (per its own javadoc, lines 177-183) — this closes the most likely trigger (a plain timeout) before it ever reaches the catch block; (b) reaching the described double-pay additionally requires the retried call to ALSO fail/except (not just the original), which is a compound, lower-probability event than the finding implies.
findings.new_evidence: Read RazorpayXClient.initiatePayout (117-160): confirms request always carries reference_id/X-Payout-Idempotency = the caller-supplied idempotencyKey, consistent with the sweep's stated mitigation. No PayoutReconciliationServiceTest scenario for the 'retry-also-fails-after-original-actually-succeeded' race was found (searched for but did not find a test exercising this specific interleaving), so the residual risk is not test-covered either way — did not execute a live-money test per safety rules.
findings.caveats: This remains a legitimate financial-correctness gap worth fixing (a terminal-state guard on Payout.confirmStatus, or a real GET-payout-status check before reversing on exception, would close it), but it is not the clean 'either stranded or double-paid' inevitability the finding states, and the specific 'failed status' premise is factually wrong for this integration.

findings.title: AdminCreatorAgentController#setMonthlyCap performs no role-tier or MFA check
findings.reason: The finding's original disagreement note ('the service method was not read, so this is unconfirmed') is resolved by reading it: it is confirmed. `setMonthlyCap` (AdminCreatorAgentController.java:52-59) has no annotation, no principal-role check, and passes straight through to `CreatorAgentPreferencesService.adminSetMonthlyCapOverride` (266-283), which validates only that the cap is non-negative and the creator profile exists — it never looks at the caller at all. The class's own javadoc rationalizes this as 'admin auth is enforced structurally by SecurityConfig's hasRole("ADMIN") matcher ... no per-method check needed here', but that matcher (SecurityConfig.java:276-277, `.requestMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")`) checks only the coarse JWT authority derived from `UserType` (AuthPrincipal.java:41-42: `"ROLE_" + userType.name()`), and `UserType` has a single generic `ADMIN` value — it does NOT encode `AdminRole` (SUPER_ADMIN/ADMIN/SUPPORT), which is a separate, finer-grained enum read only at the service layer. AdminAuthService documents that MFA is required at login only for SUPER_ADMIN/ADMIN tier and SUPPORT is explicitly EXEMPT from MFA entirely. The codebase has an established, named convention for exactly this situation — `AdminContextService.requireRoleWithMfaSatisfied(principal, allowedRoles...)`, whose own javadoc states 'this is the variant every privileged (SUPER_ADMIN/ADMIN-tier) mutating or sensitive-read endpoint should call' — and it is used across most other Admin*Service classes, but `CreatorAgentPreferencesService`/`AdminCreatorAgentController` never calls `AdminContextService` at all (confirmed by grep). The existing unit test (`AdminCreatorAgentControllerTest`) itself documents this gap in its own class comment ('Admin auth itself is enforced structurally ... no MockMvc/spring-security-test harness') and calls `controller.setMonthlyCap(null, ...)` with a null principal, which succeeds — consistent with there being no code path that would reject it.
findings.new_evidence: Confirmed via grep that `CreatorAgentPreferencesService.java` and `AdminCreatorAgentController.java` are absent from the list of classes calling `AdminContextService` (which AdminBillingService, AdminFinanceService, and most other sensitive Admin*Service classes DO call), establishing this is a deviation from the codebase's own security convention rather than an intentional low-sensitivity design choice. Net effect: a logged-in SUPPORT-tier admin (password-only, MFA-exempt by design) or any other admin tier can call `PUT /admin/creator-agent/creators/{creatorId}/monthly-cap` for any creator with no additional check, exactly as the finding claims.
findings.caveats: Did not execute a live authenticated HTTP request against a running instance (out of scope/unsafe per task rules); this is a full static trace across the security filter chain, principal/role model, and the sole service method, with no counter-evidence found and one corroborating test-comment.
